lines: The thunder rattled every hook on the wall, but nobody near the dock was hurt.
Lightning struck close enough to lift the hair on my arms.
We pulled the boats high and waited under a proper roof.
One mooring snapped in the wind. The other knots held.
The rain filled three empty barrels before the storm moved east.
A bolt hit the far bank and threw mud into the river.
The children are safe, though none of them will sleep through thunder tonight.
I counted the seconds between flash and thunder until they began getting longer.
The dock took a beating, but the pilings are still straight.
We found a loose boat downstream after the sky cleared.
Every gull vanished before the first drop fell. Sensible birds for once.
The storm churned the shallows brown and scattered the traps.
I kept everyone away from the water until the last rumble faded.
A roof tile landed in my fish barrel. Nothing else came through.
The nets are soaked, the ropes are muddy, and we are all alive.
Thunder woke the whole village before dawn.
The wind drove rain under doors facing the river.
We will need to replace one plank where lightning split the rail.
The lake stayed rough long after the clouds passed.
Next time the clouds turn green, we leave the dock sooner.
I checked the tarred rope and dry dock planks first. One spark there could take everything.
We formed a bucket line from the river before the second roof caught.
Smoke settled low by the bank and made it hard to see who needed help.
I soaked the nets and threw them over the nearest wall.
The fire never reached the boats, though the heat blistered their paint.
We carried children to the shore where the air was clearer.
A burning beam fell across the path, so we brought water around by boat.
The river gave us all the water we needed. Getting it uphill was the hard part.
I lost a barrel and two coils of rope. That is cheaper than losing a home.
The wind pushed sparks toward the dry grass until we soaked a line ahead of them.
Everyone by the dock answered when I called their name.
Wet wool over the mouth helped more than I expected in that smoke.
We found one ember hiding under the fish racks after midnight.
The cats came back once the roofs stopped glowing.
I used my best bucket until the handle split.
The fire scorched the pier, but the supports held.
We kept the wells clear for drinking and drew fire water from the river.
Someone saved my kettle. I would rather they had saved the good net.
The village smells of ash, though morning rain helped.
We are rebuilding with more space between the ovens and the timber.
During the raid, the nets could wait. Getting everyone behind a door mattered more.
I cut a mooring so the raiders could not use my boat.
We hid two families in the boathouse until the bells stopped.
Crossbow bolts punched holes through a net hanging by the lane.
The river gave us one clear route away from the fighting.
I kept the children low behind the fish barrels.
A raider tried the dock and slipped on the wet boards.
We used oars to bar the boathouse door.
The catch spoiled while we fought. Nobody complained.
I saw the banner fall, then heard our people cheering from the square.
We ferried the injured across the river where the fighting was lighter.
One boat came back with arrows in the hull and water at the ankles.
The bells carried farther over the water than any shouted warning.
I have never been happier to see iron golems near my nets.
We counted villagers before we counted damage.
The raiders took food from a barrel and missed the people hiding behind it.
I kept a knife for rope in one hand and a shield in the other.
The shore is quiet again, but I still look up when I hear a crossbow.
We found bolts buried in the dock all the way to the end.
The village held. Tomorrow I will mend what the raid tore.
Something tested the boathouse latch after midnight. We have replaced it with iron.
The warning bell pulled us out of sleep before the monsters reached the dock.
I lit every lantern along the water so nobody ran into the river.
We moved the children away from windows facing the dark bank.
A drowned came up beside the boats while the rest attacked from the road.
The moon gave us enough light to see movement between the houses.
I woke to claws on the door and an oar already in my hands.
Nobody slept again after the first scream.
We checked every shed at sunrise before letting people outside.
The dark made the attack feel larger than it was.
I heard splashing behind me and nearly swung at a floating log.
One lantern went out at the worst possible moment.
We tied a rope between the boathouse and the square so people could follow it in the dark.
The dogs barked before any villager heard the footsteps.
I kept the cooking fire low so our eyes stayed used to darkness.
By dawn, the shore was littered with arrows and broken boards.
The attack ended quickly, but the silence afterward lasted hours.
We are adding shutters to the windows near the bank.
I found tracks circling the fish racks where someone had been watching.
Tonight we sleep in turns until we know the danger has passed.
The wind threw sand through every crack. I am still finding it in the barrels.
We covered our faces and followed the wall back from the dock.
The river disappeared behind a brown curtain before noon.
I tied every loose crate down before the worst gusts arrived.
Sand stripped the paint from the side of the boat.
Nobody went near the water once we lost sight of the bank.
The storm buried the lower half of the fish racks.
We dampened cloth for our mouths and stayed inside.
A roof panel sailed past like a badly thrown net.
The wind moved enough sand to block the boathouse door.
I could hear the dock creaking but could not see it from ten steps away.
We counted voices in the dark because faces were impossible to find.
The catch ended up seasoned before it reached the kitchen.
Sand packed into every knot and hinge along the shore.
The sky turned orange, then nearly black.
We found one missing crate against the well after the storm.
My eyes still sting from checking the moorings.
The boats survived because we pulled them onto dry ground early.
We are clearing the paths before the next wind piles them shut again.
I would take a week of rain over another hour of that dust.
We cleared a path from every house to the well before the snow rose higher.
The nets froze stiff enough to stand on their own.
I brought the boats ashore before ice closed around them.
Warm food mattered more than any work waiting outside.
The wind erased our footprints between the dock and the square.
We tied guide ropes along the paths so nobody wandered into the whiteout.
One chimney blocked with snow, so we moved that family before smoke filled the room.
The river kept moving under a skin of loose ice.
I found a drift taller than the boathouse door.
Everyone with dry wood shared it without counting.
The children slept near the largest hearth while adults took watch.
Snow packed under the roof tiles and melted into the loft.
We broke ice from the water trough twice before morning.
The fish stayed frozen without a cellar for once.
A warm bowl did more for morale than any brave speech.
I checked on the oldest villagers before digging out my own door.
The storm took one small roof and spared every life.
We marked the river edge with poles before the ground disappeared.
It is quiet now, except for shovels and dripping eaves.
The paths are open again, but nobody should travel alone yet.
